v1.feedback: The parity-violation concept is elegantly mapped — left-side radioactive decay with Cerenkov blue-grey shift is a genuinely physics-literate surprise. Palette is impeccable (ink-on-parchment, no saturation issues). Two refinements: (1) the calyx bowl is shallow (y = -0.15*r²) viewed from z=12, so the interference bands may read as a flat disc rather than a dimensional form — consider tilting the default camera slightly (camera.position.set(0, 2, 11)) or deepening the bowl curvature so the 6-petal scallop reads as volume, not just texture; (2) the violation/recovery cycle timing is critical — if the decay threshold ramps too fast the left side just vanishes, too slow and you miss it; expose the cycle period and test that the asymmetry is clearly visible for at least 3-4 seconds before recovery begins.

v2.feedback: The parity-violation concept is genuinely strong — symmetry-breaking as temporal narrative on a Riley calyx is a smart surprise swerve. No banned techniques detected: no autoRotate, no camera jitter, no fast rotation. The warm earth-tone background (#faf2dd → #6e4926) and CSS grain overlay are excellent. Two concerns: (1) the fragment shader is truncated so I cannot verify the 'Čerenkov blue-ash' violation color stays below 65% HSL saturation — if that cold shift reads as vivid or neon blue, it triggers a hard penalty, so clamp it firmly toward slate/ash/gunmetal rather than anything that reads as electric blue; (2) the 6-petal calyx bowl, while mathematically structured, risks reading as a shallow dish from the tilted camera at z=10.5 — the -0.35*r² curvature may not produce enough visible depth at 38° FOV. Consider deepening the bowl coefficient to -0.55 or pulling the camera slightly higher (y≈3.5) so the scallop ridges cast visible parallax shadows, making the form unmistakably three-dimensional before the violation event begins.
